title: MB9-25603
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I allow the appeal.
The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Mexico. The appellant fears for his life in his country of origin after he reported members of a street gang who killed his brother in 2015.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the appellant's refugee protection claim because he did not establish that his brother had died at the hands of a criminal gang that had punished him for wanting to leave the gang. The RPD concluded that the risk the appellant would face if he returned to Mexico is generalized.

On appeal, the appellant submits that the RPD erred by not finding him credible and that it made a number of errors in its analysis of his situation, in particular by neglecting to perform an individualized assessment of his subjective fear and his prospective risk in Mexico.
The determinative issue in this appeal is the prospective risk. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the appellant(s) is accepted/rejected

In accordance with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act,1 I may accept only evidence i. that arose after the RPD rendered its decision, ii. that was not reasonably available at the time of the decision, or iii. that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented to the RPD before the decision was rendered.
If the evidence satisfies one or more of these requirements, I must decide whether it is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.2

Although the appellant's counsel states in his notice of appeal that new evidence is not being presented, paragraph 50 of the memorandum announces the inclusion of three new items of documentary evidence concerning criminal groups in Mexico: - An article from Le Journal Lutte OuvriÒre entitled, "Mexique : narcotrafic et dÕliquescence de l'ètat" [Mexico: drug trafficking and failure of the state], dated October 23, 2019. - An article from Le Journal de MontrÕal entitled, "Mexique : neuf morts dans une fusillade entre gangs dans le sud" [Mexico: 9 dead in a gang shooting in the south], dated October 24, 2019. - An article from LibÕration entitled, "Mexique, une ville terrorisÕe par un cartel, qui libÒre un fils d'El Chapo" [Mexico, a city terrorized by a cartel releases one of El Chapo's sons], dated October 18, 2019.

This new evidence is accepted since the articles were all published after the RPD rendered its decision on October 7, 2019. As a result, they were not available at the time of the decision and they could not have been presented before the RPD rendered its decision.
My role is to examine all of the evidence and determine whether the RPD's decision is correct.3

The appellant states that on XXXX XXXX, 2015, his brother was beaten by members of a street gang because he no longer wanted to be part of this criminal gang. The appellant's brother's injuries included XXXX XXXX XXXX and he was hospitalized, but he never regained consciousness. On XXXX XXXX, 2015, the appellant's brother died of his injuries. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, the appellant reported the perpetrators of the assault against his brother, but his mother had the investigation stopped because she was too afraid that the pandillas would seek revenge. The appellant then moved several times to different states in Mexico because he feared reprisals from the street gangs for reporting them and because individuals were looking for him. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, the appellant left Mexico for Canada.

The RPD found the appellant credible regarding his brother's death but concluded that he had not established a personalized prospective risk. The appellant's testimony is corroborated by testimony from his sister and by several exhibits on the appellant's record, including his brother's death certificate and the report on the collection of the body issued by Mexico's Secretariat of Health.

The Federal Court of Appeal, in Maldonado,4 states that when a refugee protection claimant swears to the truth of certain facts, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is a valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. The RPD found the appellant credible, and I took this into consideration in my analysis of the internal flight alternative. Uncertainty as to the identity of the agent of harm

The RPD drew negative inferences with regard to the appellant's credibility because he could not identify, by name, the gang that killed his brother. For the panel, [translation] "The claimant's inability to identify a particular gang, one he fears and that was responsible for his brother death, instead suggests that the claimant wanted to embellish his story to obtain refugee protection."

In my view, given that the appellant is credible with regard to his brother's death, that this testimony is corroborated by considerable evidence and that the appellant gave spontaneous and very detailed testimony,5 I find the appellant credible with regard to his fear in Mexico.

At the hearing, the appellant clearly stated that he feared the street gangs involved in his brother's death. Moreover, contrary to what the RPD indicates in its decision, the appellant identified the agent of harm.

The appellant stated, several times,6 that the street gangs in the Federal District work for the Jalisco Nueva Generaciµn (CJNG) or the Familia Michoacana cartels and that he fears these cartels. In addition, the appellant stated that he fears two individuals in particular that belong to these cartels.7 The RPD did not consider this part of the appellant's testimony. The appellant's Basis of Claim Form also clearly indicates that the appellant fears specific individuals, namely the individuals who forced his brother to go out with them every night when he wanted to leave the gang.

The circumstances of the appellant's brother's death are corroborated by the medical report submitted in evidence, which clearly states that the death of the appellant's brother is the result of a crime. The appellant's detailed complaint to the police also confirms the circumstances of his brother's death.
The RPD erred in concluding that the appellant did not identify the agent of harm. Prospective risk

The appellant attempted to relocate elsewhere in Mexico prior to claiming refugee protection in Canada. However, he left his country after the individuals he fears were still looking for him and had located one of his family members. At the hearing, the appellant testified that he does not know the names of the two individuals he fears but that he could identify them and vice versa. He also testified that he fears for his life everywhere in Mexico.8

Applying the presumption of truthfulness and considering the documentary evidence, I find the appellant's testimony credible, including as it relates to his claim that he would be in danger in Mexico.
The appellant has established a prospective risk should he return to Mexico. The appellant has no internal flight alternative in Mexico

Like the appellant, I note that the documentary evidence states that organized crime is present throughout Mexico. The documentary evidence also indicates that the CJNG and Familia Michoacana cartels have a presence everywhere in Mexico.

A recent study by the United States Library of Congress states that the CJNG is expanding in Mexico and is one of the largest and most violent cartels.9 The same document indicates that the Mexican government considers the CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in Mexico and one of two with the most extensive reach: In 2015, the Mexican government declared CJNG one of the most dangerous cartels in the country and one of two with the most extensive reach. In October 2016, the U.S. Department of the Treasury echoed the Mexican government when it described the group as one of the world's "most prolific and violent drug trafficking organizations." According to some analysts, CJNG has operations throughout the Americas, Asia, and Europe. The group allegedly is responsible for distributing cocaine and methamphetamine along "10,000 kilometres of the Pacific Coast in a route that extends from the Southern Cone to the border of the United States and Canada." To best understand CJNG's international reach, it is important to first consider its expansion within Mexico. In 2016, many analysts maintained the cartel had presence throughout the country in a combined area that made up nearly half of Mexico. Recent reports indicate the group has pushed further into Aguas Calientes, San Luis Potosi, and Zacatecas states. The group has battled Los Zetas and Gulf Cartel factions in Tabasco, Veracruz, and Guanajuato, and it has battled the Sinaloa federation in the Baja peninsulas and Chihuahua. CJNG's ambitious expansion campaign has led to high levels of violence, particularly in Ciudad Juarez and Tijuana, where it has clashed with the Sinaloa federation for control of the lucrative heroin trade and corresponding smuggling routes. The group has also been linked to several mass graves in southwestern Mexico and was responsible for shooting down an army helicopter in 2015, the first successful takedown of a military asset of its kind in Mexico.10

According to the documentary evidence, the CJNG has a strong presence in 24 of the 32 Mexican states, and in all 32 states when alliances with other cartels are included.11. The evidence also states that the CJNG allies with the La Familia cartel.12

Considering that members of the appellant's family have been contacted and that the individuals he fears have looked for him, it can be concluded that they have the motivation and the ability to find him. The fact that the appellant can identify the individuals who killed his brother, and vice versa, is another reason that could motivate the cartels to track him down. In my opinion, on a balance of probabilities, this is still a possibility because the CJNG still has the means to locate the appellant and the motivation to do so, since its reputation depends in part on its ability to make people like the appellant's brother, who refuse to work for the cartel, disappear.13

Applying the presumption of truthfulness and considering the documentary evidence, I find the appellant's testimony credible, including as it relates to his claim that he would be at risk everywhere in Mexico.

Accordingly, on a balance of probabilities, there is a serious possibility that the appellant would be persecuted and/or subjected to a risk to his life or to a risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Mexico. No adequate state protection
While states are presumed capable of protecting their citizens, I am of the opinion that the appellant does not have access to adequate state protection in Mexico.
The appellant left Mexico because he believed that the state authorities would not be able to protect him from the individuals he fears.
The documentary evidence refers to ties between CJNG members and corrupt Mexican authorities. The documentary evidence confirms that state authorities are often in collusion with the cartels.14

The United States Department of State reports that police, military and other government officials are sometimes involved with criminal organizations in murders, disappearances, torture and arbitrary detentions.15

A recent study states that the CJNG has sufficient power to corrupt or even confront the Mexican state with impunity.16 The same document reports that the CJNG engages in large-scale corruption. For example, one sources states that half the Guadalajara municipal police force is on the CJNG's payroll.17
I consider the appellant's testimony and the documentary evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption of state protection.

On a balance of probabilities, I conclude that the appellant would be personally subjected to a risk to his life in Mexico. I conclude that he cannot avail himself of Mexico's protection. The appellant faces a personalized risk to his life in every part of Mexico.

The appeal is allowed. I substitute the RPD's determination with my own determination that the appellant is a person in need of protection.
